chapters.name: Chapter 1: Your path to an insurance license

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What an agent does and which license line you need
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose the license line that fits the insurance job you want.
This lesson builds toward: Given an insurance job or product, you will identify which license line and which role fits it, getting at least 5 of 6 examples right.
An insurance agent, called a producer in the law, sells, solicits or negotiates insurance for customers. Every state requires a license to do this. A captive agent sells for one company. An independent agent sells for several companies and often runs a small business. An agent must also be appointed by each insurance company they sell for.
States issue licenses by line of authority. The four most common major lines are Life, Accident and Health (sickness), Property and Casualty. Many people start with Life and Health together, or with Property and Casualty together. Some states also offer a smaller Personal Lines license for home and car insurance only.
Life covers death and some long-term savings policies. Accident and Health covers medical bills, disability income and similar costs. Property covers damage to things you own, like a house or car. Casualty covers liability, which is the money you owe if you hurt someone or damage their things.
Other insurance jobs use a different license. An adjuster investigates and settles claims. Selling some investment-type products, such as variable annuities, also needs a securities license. Check your state's list of license types before you pay for any course.
Words to know:
- Producer: the legal word for a licensed insurance agent or broker who sells insurance.
- Line of authority: a type of insurance your license lets you sell, such as Life or Property.
- Appointment: an insurance company's official approval for you to sell its products.
- Liability: the money you legally owe someone if you injure them or damage their property.
- Adjuster: a person who investigates and settles insurance claims; usually a separate license.
Try it now: Write down three insurance jobs you could apply for (for example a call-center agent selling car insurance, a bank employee selling life insurance, or your own agency). Next to each, write the license line or lines it needs.
You can now say what an insurance producer does and choose the license line that fits a job.

check.q: A job ad says you will sell car and homeowners insurance. Which license lines fit?
check.why: Car and home policies cover damage to property and liability to others, which are Property and Casualty.

options: An agent who sells for only one insurance company
An agent who only settles claims
An agent who works for the state
check.why: A captive agent represents one company; an independent agent represents several.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Finding your state's official licensing steps
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Find your state's licensing steps, testing company and exam outline on official pages.
This lesson builds toward: For your own state, you will find the official licensing steps, the testing company and the exam content outline, writing down each step with its official web address.
Your state's insurance department makes the rules. To find it, use the NAIC (National Association of Insurance Commissioners) page that links to every state department. Look for pages named producer licensing, agent licensing or how to apply.
Most states follow a similar path: a prelicensing course (required in many states, not all), a state exam given by a testing company, fingerprints or a background check, an application, and then an appointment by an insurer. After you are licensed, you renew it and take continuing education. For example, Texas, when we checked in October 2026, gave its exam through Pearson VUE, required fingerprints, and took applications through Sircon or NIPR only after you pass the exam.
The testing company publishes a candidate handbook and an exam content outline for your state. The outline lists every topic and how many questions come from each. It is the most useful study tool you have, and it is free.
If you have a criminal record, be honest on the application. A federal law (18 U.S.C. 1033) says a person convicted of a felony involving dishonesty or breach of trust needs the written consent of an insurance regulator to work in insurance. Your state department explains how to ask. Do not let a course seller tell you it does not matter.
Step by step:
- Open the NAIC state insurance departments page and choose your state.
- Find the producer or agent licensing page and the list of license types.
- Write down each step: prelicensing education, exam, fingerprints, application, appointment.
- Find the testing company's name and download the free candidate handbook and content outline.
- Write down the official web address for each step and the date you checked it.
Words to know:
- NAIC: National Association of Insurance Commissioners: the group of state insurance regulators.
- Prelicensing education: a course some states require before you may take the license exam.
- Content outline: the list of exam topics and how many questions come from each.
- NIPR: National Insurance Producer Registry: a website many states use for license applications and renewals.
- Continuing education: classes licensed agents must take to renew their license.
Official sources:
- NAIC: Find your state insurance department
- NIPR: National Insurance Producer Registry (apply for and renew producer licenses)
- Texas Department of Insurance: Agent licenses
- Texas Department of Insurance: How to apply for a general lines life, accident, health and HMO license
- 18 U.S.C. 1033 (Cornell Legal Information Institute)
Try it now: Open the NAIC page, choose your state and find its producer licensing page. Write each licensing step in order, the testing company's name, and the web address of the exam content outline.
You can now find your state's official licensing steps, testing company and exam content outline.

check.q: Where do you find the real licensing steps for your state?
options: An ad for a prelicensing course
Your state insurance department's official page
A friend licensed in another state
check.why: Each state's insurance department sets and publishes its own licensing rules.

check.q: Which free document tells you what topics are on your state's exam?
options: The testing company's exam content outline
check.why: The content outline lists every exam topic and how many questions come from each.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Core terms and how an insurance contract works
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Explain the core insurance terms and contract ideas in your own words.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of exam words and ideas, you will explain core insurance terms and contract principles in plain words, with the right meaning for at least 8 of 10.
Insurance moves risk from a person to an insurance company. The insured pays a premium. In return, the insurer promises to pay for certain losses. The policy is the written contract, and the declarations page lists who and what is covered, the limits and the premium.
Exams test a few big ideas. Insurable interest: you must stand to lose money if the loss happens. Indemnity: insurance puts you back where you were, not better off. Utmost good faith: both sides must be honest, so a lie on an application (misrepresentation) can void coverage. Underwriting: the insurer studies the risk and decides whether to accept it and at what price.
An insurance policy is a contract, so it needs an offer and acceptance, consideration (the premium and the promise), competent parties and a legal purpose. It is also a contract of adhesion: the insurer writes it and the customer accepts it as written, so unclear wording is usually read in the customer's favor.
Learn these words with flash cards. Exams often give a short story and ask which idea it shows.
Words to know:
- Premium: the money the insured pays for coverage.
- Insurable interest: having a real money loss if the insured event happens.
- Indemnity: paying back the loss so you end up where you were, not better off.
- Underwriting: studying a risk to decide whether to insure it and at what price.
- Declarations page: the page of a policy that lists who is covered, what is covered, limits and premium.
- Contract of adhesion: a contract written by one side and accepted as is by the other.
Try it now: Make 10 flash cards on paper or a phone: one side the word (premium, insurable interest, indemnity, underwriting, declarations page, consideration, adhesion, misrepresentation, insured, insurer), the other side your own one-line meaning. Test yourself until you get 8 of 10.
You can now explain the core insurance words and the parts of an insurance contract in plain words.

check.q: A man wants to buy fire insurance on a stranger's house. Which idea stops him?
check.why: He would lose no money if the stranger's house burned, so he has no insurable interest.

check.q: After a covered theft, the insurer pays the value of the stolen TV, not a bigger TV. Which idea is this?
check.why: Indemnity puts the insured back where they were, not better off.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Life and health basics and the health claim math
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate who pays what on a practice health claim with a deductible and coinsurance.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of exam words and ideas, you will explain core insurance terms and contract principles in plain words, with the right meaning for at least 8 of 10. Given a practice claim with a deductible, coinsurance or a policy limit, you will calculate how much the insurer pays and how much the insured pays, correct to the dollar on 3 practice claims.
Life insurance: term life covers a set number of years and has no cash value. Permanent life, such as whole life, can last for life and builds cash value. The beneficiary is the person who gets the death benefit; a contingent beneficiary gets it if the first one has died. The policyowner controls the policy and may be a different person from the insured.
Health insurance has its own words. The deductible is what you pay each year before the plan starts sharing costs. Coinsurance is the percent you share after that, such as 80/20: the plan pays 80% and you pay 20%. A copay is a set dollar amount for a visit. The out-of-pocket maximum is the most you pay in a year for covered care.
Practice only, made-up numbers: a $3,000 covered bill, a $1,000 deductible not yet met, 80/20 coinsurance. You pay the first $1,000. The remaining $2,000 is shared: the plan pays 80% ($1,600) and you pay 20% ($400). You pay $1,400 in total; the plan pays $1,600. Check: $1,400 + $1,600 = $3,000.
Step by step:
- Write the covered bill amount.
- Subtract the part of the deductible still owed; the insured pays that part.
- Split what is left by the coinsurance percents.
- Add the insured's deductible and coinsurance; stop at the out-of-pocket maximum.
- Check that the two shares add up to the bill.
Words to know:
- Beneficiary: the person who receives the money when the insured person dies.
- Cash value: savings built inside a permanent life policy.
- Deductible: the amount you pay before the insurance starts to pay.
- Coinsurance: the percent of the cost you share with the plan after the deductible.
- Out-of-pocket maximum: the most you pay in a plan year for covered care.
Try it now: Practice only: work this claim on paper. A $5,000 covered bill, a $500 deductible not yet met, 80/20 coinsurance. How much does the insured pay, and how much does the plan pay? (Answer: insured $500 + $900 = $1,400; plan $3,600.)
You can now explain the main life and health insurance words and work a health claim with a deductible and coinsurance.

check.q: Practice only: a $2,000 covered bill, a $500 deductible not yet met, 80/20 coinsurance. What does the insured pay?
check.why: $500 deductible plus 20% of the remaining $1,500 ($300) is $800.

check.q: Which life insurance policy builds cash value?
check.why: Permanent policies like whole life build cash value; term policies do not.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Property and casualty basics and the property claim math
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate what a property or auto liability policy pays on a practice claim.
This lesson builds toward: Given an insurance job or product, you will identify which license line and which role fits it, getting at least 5 of 6 examples right. Given a practice claim with a deductible, coinsurance or a policy limit, you will calculate how much the insurer pays and how much the insured pays, correct to the dollar on 3 practice claims.
Property policies pay for damage to things you own. Replacement cost pays to replace the item with a new one of like kind. Actual cash value pays replacement cost minus depreciation (wear and age). Practice only: a sofa costs $1,200 new and has $500 of depreciation, so its actual cash value is $700. A deductible comes off the payment.
Casualty (liability) coverage pays others when you are legally responsible for harming them. Auto liability limits are often written as three numbers, such as 25/50/25: up to $25,000 for one person's injuries, up to $50,000 for all injuries in one accident, and up to $25,000 for property damage. Your state sets the minimums; check them.
Practice only: a driver with 25/50/25 limits injures one person, whose bills are $40,000. The policy pays $25,000, its per-person limit. The driver may have to pay the other $15,000 personally. That is why agents explain limits carefully.
Step by step:
- Find the loss amount and the type of coverage.
- For actual cash value, subtract depreciation from replacement cost.
- Subtract the deductible.
- Compare with the policy limit; the insurer never pays more than the limit.
- Anything above the limit is the insured's to pay.
Words to know:
- Replacement cost: the cost to replace an item with a new one of like kind and quality.
- Actual cash value: replacement cost minus depreciation.
- Depreciation: the loss in value from age and wear.
- Policy limit: the most the insurer will pay for a covered loss.
- Split limits: auto liability limits written as three numbers, like 25/50/25.
Try it now: Practice only: a kitchen fire causes $18,000 of covered damage. The homeowners policy pays replacement cost, the deductible is $1,000, and the dwelling limit is $250,000. Write what the insurer pays and what the homeowner pays. (Answer: insurer $17,000; homeowner $1,000.)
You can now tell property from casualty coverage and work practice claims with depreciation, deductibles and limits.

check.q: Practice only: a TV costs $900 new and has $300 of depreciation. What is its actual cash value?
check.why: Actual cash value is replacement cost minus depreciation: $900 - $300 = $600.

check.q: A customer accidentally injures a delivery driver at home and is sued. Which kind of coverage responds?
check.why: Liability coverage pays others when the insured is legally responsible for harming them.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Ethics rules and your study-and-test plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Spot unethical sales practices and write a dated study-and-test plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given a sales or service situation, you will spot unethical or illegal practices and choose the honest action, getting at least 4 of 5 situations right. Using your state's official steps and exam outline, you will write a dated study-and-test plan for your license exam, covering every official step, every outline topic and at least two practice-test dates.
States have unfair trade practice laws, and every exam tests them. Misrepresentation is lying about or hiding what a policy does. Twisting is talking a customer into replacing a policy with a lie or a misleading comparison, to their harm. Churning is replacing policies again and again mainly to earn new commissions. Rebating is giving part of your commission or a gift to get a sale; it is illegal in many states, so check your state's rule. Premiums you collect belong to the customer and insurer: an agent holds them in trust (a fiduciary duty) and must not mix them with personal money (commingling).
Honest action is simple: tell the truth about coverage, put the customer's needs first, compare policies fairly, write things down, and keep premium money separate. If you are not sure, ask your manager or the state department.
Now plan. Use your state's content outline to list each topic and its number of questions. Give more study days to the heavy topics. Set a target exam date, two or more practice-test dates and a score goal. Finish any required prelicensing course before you book the exam. Read every exam question twice and watch for words like EXCEPT and NOT.
Final task: write your one-page Study-and-Test Plan with your license line, your state's official steps with web addresses, the outline topics and weights, a dated weekly schedule, practice-test dates, three practice claims and three ethics rules.
Step by step:
- List your state's official steps in order with their web addresses.
- Copy each outline topic and its number of questions.
- Give more study days to the topics with the most questions.
- Pick a target exam date and at least two practice-test dates with a score goal.
- Add three practice claims and three ethics rules in your own words.
Words to know:
- Misrepresentation: lying about or hiding what a policy does or costs.
- Twisting: using lies or misleading comparisons to get a customer to replace a policy.
- Churning: replacing policies again and again mainly to earn commissions.
- Rebating: giving back part of a commission or a gift to win a sale; illegal in many states.
- Fiduciary: a person trusted to handle someone else's money honestly.
- Commingling: mixing customer premium money with your own money.
Official sources:
- NAIC Model Law 880: Unfair Trade Practices Act
- NAIC: Find your state insurance department
Try it now: Final task: write your Insurance License Study-and-Test Plan on one page, using your state's official steps and content outline, with real dates for each study week, two practice tests and your target exam date.
You can now spot unethical sales practices, choose the honest action, and follow a dated study-and-test plan for your license exam.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Right license line No line named, or a line that does not fit the job. Names the license line that fits the job and says why. Also names a second line or license the learner may need later and why. Official steps Steps are missing or come from ads or friends. Every step from the state's official page, in order, with web addresses. Adds the date checked, the testing company's handbook and any background-check steps. Outline topics and terms No outline topics, or core terms explained wrongly. Lists every outline topic with its weight and explains the key terms correctly. Flags the learner's weakest topics and adds flash cards for them. Practice claims Fewer than three claims, or wrong answers. Three practice claims worked correctly, showing each step. Claims cover a deductible, coinsurance and a policy limit, each with a check of the math. Ethics rules Rules missing or wrong. Three ethics rules explained correctly in the learner's own words. Each rule comes with a short example of the honest action. Dated plan No dates, or no practice tests. A weekly schedule with dates, a target exam date and two practice tests with a score goal. More study days go to the heaviest outline topics, with a backup exam date. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: An agent tells a senior her old policy is "worthless" so she will buy a new one that pays the agent more. What is this?
check.why: Using a misleading claim to get a customer to replace a policy is twisting.

check.q: Your state's outline gives one topic far more questions than the others. What do you do in your plan?
options: Give that topic more study days
Skip it because it is long
check.why: Topics with more questions earn more study time.
